# Continuous Integration on Other Forges {#sec-ci-other-forges}

@sec-verification writes its workflows for GitHub Actions.
This appendix carries the same three gates and the verify
job to GitLab CI. It then takes up two design questions
for a compendium that must run on more than one forge:
where the checking logic should live, and whether a
workflow should configure itself from the files present.
It assumes the gates, the verify job, and the
scripts `ci/dependency-gate.R` and `ci/run-tests.R` of
@sec-verification. Nothing in the core chapters depends on
it.

## Why the forge matters

Continuous integration is a general idea with several
implementations, and the choice of forge is often not the
researcher's to make. Research compendia are often
authored on institutional, self-hosted GitLab. Many
universities and laboratories run their own GitLab servers
and cannot, or will not, push a repository to github.com.
This is particularly so where data-governance rules
discourage commercial cloud hosting. For a registry study
whose data-handling agreement forbids external hosting,
running the same checks on institutional GitLab is a
precondition, not a convenience.

The two dialects differ structurally. GitHub Actions uses
one or more workflow files under `.github/workflows/`, each
organized into jobs and, within a job, a sequence of named
steps. GitLab CI uses a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` organized
into stages, each stage running a script. The difference
is one of syntax and hosting, not of principle.

## The three gates in GitLab's dialect

The same three gates, and the verify job, expressed in the
GitLab dialect look like this. As in @sec-verification, we
show a static file that GitLab executes and this book does
not; its YAML was checked for syntax only.

```yaml
stages:
  - gates
  - verify

gates:
  stage: gates
  # The tag must name the R version recorded in renv.lock.
  image: rocker/verse:4.6.1
  script:
    - Rscript -e 'renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)'
    - Rscript -e 'renv::install("rcmdcheck")'
    # Gate 1: R CMD check of the package skin
    - Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args = "--no-manual",
        error_on = "warning")'
    # Gate 2: every package used in analysis/ is pinned
    - Rscript ci/dependency-gate.R
    # Gate 3: the report re-renders from source
    - Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render(
        "analysis/report/report.Rmd",
        output_format = "html_document",
        output_dir = tempdir())'

verify:
  stage: verify
  # A shell-executor runner with Docker installed; the
  # tag is whatever the institution assigns to it.
  tags: [docker-shell]
  script:
    - docker build -t compendium:ci .
    - docker run --rm -e RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE
        -v "$PWD":/work -w /work
        compendium:ci Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

The GitLab file says what the GitHub file says in other
words. Each runs on the R version the lockfile records,
restores the pinned library into the project library, and
installs `rcmdcheck` beside it. Each then runs the three
gates from the repository root, so that every R step, and
the check subprocess it launches, sees the restored
library. The `.Rprofile` assumption of 'Where CI bugs
hide' in @sec-verification applies to both. The image tag
above names R 4.6.1 only as an example; a compendium names
the release its own lockfile records. The
`rocker/verse` image is used here because it ships pandoc,
which the render gate needs; on GitHub the `setup-pandoc`
action supplies it. Each script line is a separate shell
command, and GitLab fails the job at the first one that
exits with a nonzero status. Every gate can therefore fail
the pipeline.

The second job, `verify`, rebuilds the project image and
runs the baseline tests inside it, as
@sec-verification-l3 describes. On GitLab it needs a
runner that can build images, which is an institutional
decision. The common alternative, Docker-in-Docker,
requires a privileged runner that many institutions do not
allow.

## One logic, several forges

Maintaining a repository on whichever forge an institution
mandates is then a matter of translating the dialect, and
the checks carry over. The cost is that a workflow written
twice, once per dialect, is a workflow maintained twice.
Every future change must be made in two incompatible
formats, a standing divergence hazard.

The resolution is to single-source the logic in a neutral
place, the project's own `Makefile`. It holds one target
per gate (say `check`, `deps`, and `render`), each
carrying the commands shown above. Each forge's CI file
then shrinks to a thin shim that checks out the code and
calls `make`. The dialect differs only in its outermost
lines, the checking behavior is defined once, and the same
commands run on the analyst's own machine.

## Workflows that adapt to the repository

A workflow need not be configured by hand: it can adapt
itself to what the repository contains. In such a
presence-driven workflow, a feature is treated as present
exactly when its defining file exists. If `renv.lock` is
present, the workflow restores the pinned library;
otherwise it installs from `DESCRIPTION`. If a
`Dockerfile` or a Nix `flake.nix` is present, the workflow
builds and runs inside that environment; otherwise it runs
on the host runner. Such a workflow survives a project's
toggling of `renv` or of its container backend with no
edit, and one file can serve every archetype and every
capture level.

The workflows of @sec-verification are not written that
way. They assume a compendium with both a lockfile and a
`Dockerfile`, so that every step is visible. A
presence-driven workflow wraps each step in a condition,
in GitHub's dialect `if: hashFiles('Dockerfile') != ''`,
and in GitLab's a `rules: exists:` clause. That
convenience has a cost. A condition is also a way for a
gate to disappear without notice, since a misnamed file
switches the step off and the run stays green. A workflow
that adapts should therefore print which gates it ran and
which it skipped.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## With zzcollab

Setting the forge with `zzc config set-local forge gitlab`
and then running `zzc add cicd` installs a presence-driven
`.gitlab-ci.yml` with a check stage and a render stage,
chosen by `exists:` rules on `flake.nix` and `Dockerfile`.
On GitHub the same command installs the Actions workflows
for the archetype. The scaffolded `Makefile` offers
targets that a shim can call, but not every target is a
gate:

- `make check-renv` runs `zzrenvcheck` with
  `auto_fix = TRUE`. On a runner it repairs `renv.lock` in
  place and reports success for the very omission the gate
  exists to catch. Its sibling `make check-renv-no-fix`
  modifies nothing and exits nonzero on failure; only that
  target is a gate.
- `make check` runs `R CMD check --as-cran`, which exits
  nonzero on an ERROR but not on a WARNING, so an
  undeclared import passes it.
- The render targets (`docker-render`, `docker-render-qmd`,
  `docker-render-book`) start a container with
  `docker run`, so they need a runner that can run Docker.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the presence-driven trap

A presence-driven workflow skips the render gate when
`if: hashFiles('report.Rmd') != ''` evaluates to false.
Describe a concrete way this condition can silently
disable the gate without anyone intending it to, and what
single habit of the workflow catches the problem.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A rename, for instance moving `report.Rmd` to
`analysis-report.Rmd` during a reorganization, or a typo
in the condition itself, makes `hashFiles()` return an
empty string. The condition then evaluates to false and
the step is skipped. The job still reports success,
because a skipped step is not a failed one. Nothing in
the build output distinguishes 'rendered successfully'
from 'did not try to render'. The habit that catches it
is having the workflow print, for every conditional step,
whether it ran or was skipped. A silent skip is then
visible in the log, even though it does not turn the
build red.
:::
:::

## Exercises

1. **Two dialects.** Take the condensed GitHub Actions
   workflow of @sec-verification and translate its `gates`
   job into the equivalent `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Identify the
   two structural differences between the dialects
   (jobs-and-steps versus stages-and-scripts, and per-file
   versus single-file configuration), and explain why
   single-sourcing the check logic in a `Makefile` would
   let both files shrink to a thin shim.

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [gates]

gates:
  stage: gates
  image: rocker/verse:4.6.1
  script:
    - Rscript -e 'renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)'
    - Rscript -e 'renv::install("rcmdcheck")'
    # Gate 1: fails on a WARNING, as error-on does on GitHub
    - Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args = "--no-manual",
        error_on = "warning")'
    # Gate 2: stops with an error if a used package is
    # not pinned
    - Rscript ci/dependency-gate.R
    # Gate 3: render inside this image, without Docker
    - Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render(
        "analysis/report/report.Rmd",
        output_format = "html_document",
        output_dir = tempdir())'
```

**The two structural differences.**

*Jobs and steps versus stages and scripts.* GitHub Actions
composes a job from reusable `uses:` steps, each a
versioned action maintained elsewhere. The workflow
therefore reads as an assembly of components. GitLab CI
defines stages containing jobs whose bodies are shell
scripts, so the pipeline reads as commands in an image.
The GitHub form is more declarative and depends on an
ecosystem of actions; the GitLab form is more direct and
depends on nothing but the image.

*Per-file versus single-file configuration.* GitHub reads
every file under `.github/workflows/`, so a project
naturally accumulates several workflows with separate
triggers. GitLab reads a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the
root, so everything is expressed in one file with rules
selecting what runs when.

**Why a Makefile shrinks both.** The differences above are
entirely about *orchestration*: what runs, in what order,
on what trigger. The check logic itself (run `R CMD
check`, scan the dependencies, render the report) is
identical in both and belongs in neither file. Putting it
behind named targets leaves each CI file a thin shim
naming the image and calling a short list of them. The
logic is then single-sourced, testable locally with the
same command CI runs, and portable to a third forge for
the cost of one more shim.

The file renders inside the `rocker/verse` image itself,
after the `renv::restore()` line, because a job whose
`image:` is `rocker/verse` has no Docker daemon.
Rendering through the project's own image belongs in a
job on a runner that can run Docker, as the `verify` job
above does. If you adapt this exercise to your own
compendium, confirm that each gate can fail.
:::
